messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Michael, a 54‑year‑old forester in a small Midwestern town, recalled the day that would forever change his life with a clarity that bordered on pain. It was early spring, and he was alone on a logging road cutting through a dense pine stand when a chainsaw‑laden skidder rolled out of control. The heavy steel frame of the skidder slid across the gravel, slamming into a fellow worker’s back and leaving the man with a shattered vertebra. Michael’s hands, still slick with oil, had barely released the chainsaw handle when the engine sputtered, and in that split second the machine’s wheels struck a loose rock, sending the skidder careening. The victim’s scream rang out, and Michael’s heart dropped to his gut. Even years later, the memory of that violent collision triggers a burning ache in his left shoulder, a somatic echo that tells him he still carries the weight of the accident. That ache becomes a portal to a broader sense of threat. Whenever he feels the pressure of muscle pain, his mind instantly zooms to the scene of the injury, and he cannot relax even in the safety of his own home. The painful sensation signals danger, and his mind interprets it as a reminder that something catastrophic could happen again. At work, walking past a group of coworkers, he watches them intently for the slightest change in posture or pace, convinced that a misplaced step could trigger a new disaster. Strangers approaching on the forest path—truck drivers, delivery riders, even a casual jogger—instantly set off alarms; their unfamiliarity feels like a potential threat even when they pose no real danger. Each of these triggers feeds into his hypervigilant state, leaving him exhausted and on edge. The same triggers also bring back vivid memories. The pain in his shoulder conjures a bodily reenactment: his arms locked in the same position he had held on the skidder, his breath shallow and ragged. When he recalls the victim’s pain and the roar of the chainsaw, a wave of rage surges through him, as if the memory is an active threat. Alongside the fury, an overwhelming grief crashes in, and Michael feels as though he has lost his sense of self. These memories in turn deepen his negative appraisals. He comes to believe that there is something inherently flawed about him; he sees the accident as a testament to his own intrinsic fault. The memory of being unable to control the chainsaw fuels the conviction that he can no longer rely on himself, and the haunting realization that he is no longer capable of the precise work that had defined his career. Each recollection reinforces the idea that the event was his fault, and this belief keeps him trapped in a loop of self‑blame and distress. In turn, the heightened sense of threat feeds back into his memories. Even when he is not in pain, the mere sight of a heavy piece of equipment or the sound of an engine can trigger the same bodily reenactment, as if his body has learned to anticipate danger from any cue associated with his trauma. This anticipatory threat keeps his mind from fully relaxing, ensuring that his memories stay vivid and immediate. The persistent threat also magnifies his negative appraisals, as he watches himself fail to maintain control and concludes that he is still defective. The cycle between triggers, threat, memory, and negative appraisal tightens, and each time it spins he feels more isolated, more exhausted, and increasingly convinced that he cannot function in the forest as he once did. Over months, Michael began to avoid certain jobs: he no longer accepted assignments that required operating large machinery or moving through dense brush alone. The avoidance, though rational on the surface, left him unemployed for weeks, and the loss of routine made him feel more powerless. His wife, Sarah, noticed the change; she saw him pacing the kitchen at night, eyes darting to the back door whenever someone passed. She tried to reassure him that no one was coming, but Michael’s gaze kept searching for danger. Their conversations grew strained, and Michael began to fear that his inability to relax would ruin their marriage. The culmination of this spiraling distress, coupled with a recent incident in which he slipped on a wet log and nearly fell into a ravine, pushed him to finally seek help. He is now most afraid that his thoughts will continue to spiral out of control and that he will lose his sense of safety and identity, yet he also hopes that therapy will teach him to stop seeing every rustle of leaves or every distant truck as a prelude to disaster.
